title: Implementing Full-Text Search in PostgreSQL with tsvector and GIN Indexes: Better Than Elasticsearch for Small Teams
seoTitle: Postgres Full-Text Search with tsvector & GIN
description: Learn how to build fast search in PostgreSQL using tsvector and GIN indexes, saving your small team the overhead of running Elasticsearch.

author.name: Aafaque Nazir
author.bio: Independent web engineer building high-performance websites, e-commerce stores, and SaaS web applications for clients across India & worldwide.

quickAnswer: PostgreSQL full-text search using tsvector data types and GIN indexes provides fast text searching out of the box, eliminating the infrastructure complexity and extra cost of running an external search engine like Elasticsearch for small teams.

faqs.question: When should I choose PostgreSQL full-text search over Elasticsearch?
faqs.answer: PostgreSQL search is ideal when your dataset fits comfortably on a single server, you are already using Postgres (or Supabase), and you want to avoid maintaining a separate cluster, syncing data pipelines, and paying extra cloud infrastructure costs.

faqs.question: What is the role of a GIN index in Postgres search?
faqs.answer: A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) stores a map of words to the database rows that contain them. This allows Postgres to look up search terms instantly without scanning every single row in the table.

faqs.question: How do I handle multi-column search in Postgres?
faqs.answer: You can combine multiple text columns using the concatenation operator '||' inside a generated column or query expression, then create a single GIN index over that combined tsvector.

sections.title: Why Small Teams Often Do Not Need Elasticsearch

sections.text: When building applications with search requirements, many developers immediately reach for Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. While those tools excel at massive, distributed log analysis and large scale multi-node clusters, they introduce significant maintenance overhead. You have to manage JVM memory tuning, sync data continuously from your primary database, and absorb extra cloud hosting bills.

If you are running a standard web application or SaaS platform with a few million rows or less, PostgreSQL has built-in full-text search capabilities that handle complex queries easily. When working on projects like [Aura Estate](/projects/15/), utilizing Supabase and native PostgreSQL features keeps the infrastructure simple, reduces points of failure, and cuts hosting costs.

sections.title: Setting Up tsvector and Generated Columns

sections.text: PostgreSQL handles text search by converting strings into a `tsvector`—a sorted list of normalized words called lexemes. Instead of computing this conversion on every single query, modern versions of Postgres allow us to store this vector directly in the table using a generated column.

sections.caption: Creating a table with a generated search vector column
sections.code:
CREATE TABLE properties (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    description TEXT NOT NULL,
    city TEXT NOT NULL,
    search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(city, '')), 'B') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'C')
    ) STORED
);

sections.title: Search Weighting Best Practice
sections.text: Assigning weights (A, B, C) ensures that matches found in the property title rank higher in search results than matches found deep within the description text.

Without an index, Postgres must perform a sequential scan, inspecting every row to check for matching lexemes. As your table grows, query times will degrade. Adding a Generalized Inverted Index (GIN) solves this by creating an inverted tree structure.

sections.caption: Creating a GIN index on the search vector
sections.code: CREATE INDEX properties_search_idx ON properties USING GIN (search_vector);

sections.title: Executing Fast Queries from Your Application

sections.text: Once your table and GIN index are in place, querying the data is straightforward. You use the `@@` operator along with `plainto_tsquery` or `websearch_to_tsquery` to parse user input safely.

sections.caption: Searching properties with relevance ranking
sections.code:
SELECT id, title, city,
    ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'luxury apartment bandra')) AS rank
FROM properties
WHERE search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'luxury apartment bandra')
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;

items: Always specify the correct language configuration (e.g., 'english') to enable proper stemming and stop-word removal.
Use generated columns so Postgres automatically updates search vectors on inserts and updates.
Always create a GIN index on your search vector column to maintain fast query response times.
Use `websearch_to_tsquery` to give users a familiar search box experience that supports quotes and minus signs without throwing syntax errors.
